source_read: PMC full text PMC6020109 (Pharmacol Rev 2018;70(3):621-660), read in the app's browser in my own tab; whole article text read (abstract through Conclusions, Abbreviations and Footnotes), Tables 1, 2 and 3 and the Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 legends read in the HTML. Also read the linked correction, PMC12164715 (Pharmacol Rev 2018;70(4):879, doi 10.1124/pr.116.015198err). Text saved to scratchpad/ket-a/s229/zanos_2018_full.txt; erratum note in scratchpad/ket-a/s229/erratum_zanos_2018.txt.

erratum_check.what_it_corrects: Only the copyright statement: the review was published under ASPET copyright but is US Government work not protected by US copyright, and the HTML and PDF were corrected to display the right copyright. Described as a compositor's error.
erratum_check.touches_anything_extracted: No. No scientific content, number, table or figure is corrected, so nothing extracted for cl_ket_mechanism_nmda_metabolites is affected. (The notice itself misprints the first author's initial as 'Zanos Z'.)

claims.overstatement: Five points go beyond the review. (1) 'Most other targets ... act at about 10 to 1000 micromolar, above the blood levels reached in people, with exceptions such as one nicotinic receptor blocked at 0.24 micromolar in frog eggs' understates the review: the review itself calls the M1 muscarinic value (IC50 5.7 uM, rat receptor in frog eggs) a clinically relevant concentration, says concentrations up to about 10 uM are within the clinically relevant range so some nicotinic subtypes may act in vivo, and argues HCN1 inhibition (EC50 8.2-15.6 uM racemic, 4.1-7.4 uM for the S form) may contribute to anaesthesia; Table 3 also lists a dopamine transporter IC50 of 4.6 uM, an L-type calcium channel IC50 of 9.2 uM (bullfrog myocytes), a sigma Ki of 0.15 uM and dehydronorketamine at the alpha7 nicotinic receptor at IC50 0.055 uM. The blood levels and the two exception figures are right; the generalisation and the single named exception are not. (2) 'two human post-mortem cortex values of 0.42 and 0.67 micromolar': the review labels those two Table 3 rows human cortex in a radioligand binding assay and does not say post-mortem; post-mortem human brain homogenates are named only for the separate Oye et al. (1992) enantiomer IC50 values (S 1.6-1.9, R 7.2-10 uM). (3) 'almost all in rodent tissue, cell lines or frog eggs': the racemic NMDA receptor rows also include guinea pig brain, dog brain and dog cortex. (4) '31% (SD 18)' and '32% (SD 6)': the review gives 31% +/- 18% and 32% +/- 6% in running text without saying whether the spread is an SD or an SE (Table 3's header says mean +/- S.E., Table 2's says S.D.), so 'SD' is the claim's own attribution. (5) 'a mouse study finding no activity at any dopamine receptor up to 10 micromolar': in Can et al. (2016) as the review reports it, the dopamine receptor panel used human receptors expressed in cells (Table 3, D1-5R row), while the mouse part was the fast-scan voltammetry showing no change in evoked accumbal dopamine release. Otherwise the wording does not overstate: it says throughout that the figures are second-hand and not appraised, keeps doses as study conditions, and does not present the animal and cell findings as shown in people.
claims.note: Numbers checked. Trapping (about 86% against >98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801), Ki 0.18-3.1 uM for the racemate in the presence of Mg2+, the phencyclidine site inside the channel pore, the Mg2+ dependence of subunit preference (Kotermanski and Johnson, 2009, reversed between Mg2+-free and 1 mM Mg2+) and the one study finding no subunit difference (Yamakura et al., 1993) are all as stated. 'About twenty studies' is fair: the sentence carrying the 0.18-3.1 uM range cites 19 reference-years from about 17 author groups. Metabolic route (CYP2B6/CYP3A4 to norketamine, then dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines), S-norketamine Ki 1.70-2.25 uM with the R form about eight times weaker (13.0-26.46 uM; 13.0/1.70 = 7.6, 26.46/2.25 = 11.8, so 'about eight times' follows the Ebert pair), (2S,6S)-HNK Ki 10.4-21.0 uM, (2R,6R)-HNK Ki >100 uM and no functional NMDA inhibition by either up to 10 uM, the four human peak plasma values with their times (204.13 +/- 101.46 ng/mL ketamine at 40 min, 73.54 +/- 31.86 norketamine at 80 min, 13.27 +/- 6.92 dehydronorketamine at 110 min, 23.19 +/- 11.88 hydroxynorketamine pair at 230 min, Table 2 'mean +/- S.D.'), the exposure comparison (hydroxynorketamine pair 1038 and 1366 against ketamine 873.5 and 975.4 h.ng/mL) and the maximum 31% occupancy after the 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion all match. I recomputed the review's own ng/mL to micromolar conversions and get the same: 204.13/237.73 = 0.859 (review 0.86), 73.54/223.70 = 0.329 (0.33), 13.27/221.68 = 0.060 (0.06), 23.19/239.70 = 0.097 (0.097), 185/237.73 = 0.778 (0.78), 1200-2400/237.73 = 5.05-10.1 (5-10). The AUC comparison holds in both unit sets (4.33 against 3.67 h.uM in major depression, 5.70 against 4.10 in bipolar depression). Who and when: the four peak values are the treatment-resistant major-depression group; the parallel bipolar group reached 177.23 +/- 53.8 ketamine, 69.96 +/- 19.98 norketamine, 50.5 +/- 27.44 dehydronorketamine and 37.59 +/- 14.23 hydroxynorketamine, so the claim's single set should be labelled as the major-depression group (the magnitude's two AUC pairs do name 'the two patient groups'). The three qualifications the claim makes are all in the review: brain levels in people are not known (Elimination, last paragraph); no published clinical study of R-ketamine in depression and none comparing the enantiomers with each other or with the racemate (Conclusions A, last paragraph); the metabolite patents (Footnotes). 'Rodent experiments almost all from the review's own authors' is right for the main reports (Zanos et al., 2016; Moaddel et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2017; Singh et al.), but the review also cites an independent supporting study (Pham et al., 2017a) and two independent non-replications (Shirayama and Hashimoto, 2018; Yang et al., 2017), which the claim could add. No dosing, route, timing or combination advice in the claim; doses appear only as study conditions. Design: narrative review with no methods or search section, consistent with the claim's second-hand framing.

anchors.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics of Ketamine and Its Metabolites > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ketamine binds the allosteric phencyclidine site inside the channel pore and blocks the receptor noncompetitively (open-channel blocker, 1st paragraph). Trapping capability about 86%, against >98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801. Binding affinity at the phencyclidine site reported between 0.18 and 3.1 micromolar in the presence of Mg2+, the sentence citing 19 reference-years (Wong 1986, 1988; MacDonald 1987; Kornhuber 1989; Reynolds and Miller 1989; Sharif 1991; Bresink 1995; Lynch 1995; Parsons 1995; Kapur and Seeman 2001, 2002; Sun and Wessinger 2004; Seeman 2005; Gilling 2009; Moaddel 2013; Bonifazi 2015; Wallach 2016; Kang 2017; Morris 2017).

anchors.locator: Table 3 (Molecular targets of ketamine and its metabolites), NMDAR rows for (R,S)-ketamine
anchors.extracted: Racemic ketamine NMDA receptor affinities: two human cortex values, Ki 0.42 +/- 0.03 (Kornhuber et al., 1989) and Ki 0.67 +/- 0.15 (Gilling et al., 2009), both radioligand [3H]MK-801 binding, with no statement that the tissue was post-mortem. The other rows are rat (cortex, brain, striatum, spinal cord, forebrain, cerebellum, synaptic membranes, cultured neurons), mouse brain, guinea pig brain, dog brain and dog cortex, HEK293 and tsA201 cells and receptors expressed in Xenopus oocytes; a further 'Human' row (Ki 1.47 +/- 0.68) is a recombinant GluN1/2A patch-clamp value, not tissue. Header: values are mean +/- S.E. unless otherwise indicated. One racemic row (Ki > 10, rat glioma hybrid NG108-15 cells, Georg and Friedl 1991) falls outside the 0.18-3.1 micromolar range given in the text, and three citations in that range sentence (MacDonald 1987, Moaddel 2013, Bonifazi 2015) have no racemic NMDA receptor row in the table.

anchors.locator: III > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 3rd paragraph (after Table 3)
anchors.extracted: Subanesthetic ketamine (40-minute intravenous infusion, 0.5 mg/kg), the antidepressant condition, gave a maximum of 31% +/- 18% NMDA receptor occupancy (Shaffer et al., 2014), similar to the 32% +/- 6% maximum estimated in rats after an antidepressant-relevant 10 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose. Whether the spread is an SD or an SE is not stated. Same paragraph: the S form has about fourfold higher affinity than the R form and twice that of the racemate (S 0.3-0.69, R 1.4-2.57, racemate 0.18-3.1 micromolar, with Mg2+ present).

Which subunits are blocked most depends on magnesium: without extracellular Mg2+ ketamine inhibits GluN1/2A (IC50 0.33 +/- 0.01) and GluN1/2B (0.31 +/- 0.02) somewhat more potently than GluN1/2C (0.51 +/- 0.01) and GluN1/2D (0.83 +/- 0.02); with 1 mM Mg2+ the order reverses (GluN1/2C 1.18, GluN1/2D 2.95, against GluN1/2A 5.35 +/- 0.34 and GluN1/2B 5.08 +/- 0.02) (Kotermanski and Johnson, 2009). Yamakura et al. (1993) found no difference between subunit combinations in Xenopus oocytes; the review concludes there is a lack of clarity on subunit selectivity. Separately, post-mortem human brain homogenates gave [3H]MK-801 displacement IC50 1.6-1.9 micromolar for the S form and 7.2-10 for the R form (Oye et al., 1992).

With extracellular Mg2+ present, norketamine also inhibits the NMDA receptor: S-norketamine Ki 1.70-2.25 micromolar, R-norketamine about eight times lower affinity (Ki 13.0-26.46) (Ebert et al., 1997; Moaddel et al., 2013); S-norketamine also inhibited NMDA-evoked currents more potently (IC50 3.0 +/- 0.8 against 39 +/- 1.4 micromolar) in rat cortical neurons.

anchors.locator: Table 3, norketamine rows, read against III > A, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The text locates the S-norketamine Ki range in spinal cord and cerebral cortex, but the table's two matching rows are rat cortex (1.7 +/- 0.050, Ebert et al., 1997) and rat whole brain (2.25 +/- 0.22, Moaddel et al., 2013), with no spinal cord row for norketamine. The table also carries a third source (Morris et al., 2017) giving S-norketamine Ki 0.87 and R-norketamine Ki 0.60, which reverses the eight-fold S-over-R order the text states.

Dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines displace [3H]MK-801 weakly or not at all: (2S,6S)-HNK Ki 10.4-21.0 micromolar, (2R,6R)-HNK no appreciable affinity (Ki > 100); up to 10 micromolar neither functionally inhibits NMDA-evoked currents in rat hippocampal interneurons (Zanos et al., 2016), confirmed for (2R,6R)-HNK by Suzuki et al. (2017), which saw about 40% inhibition only at 50 micromolar without Mg2+ (ketamine >90% at the same concentration). R-dehydronorketamine 59.7-74.6 and S-dehydronorketamine 39.0-42.0 micromolar. Table 3 gives (2S,6S)-HNK Ki values of 21.19, >10 and 7.34 with an IC50 of 10.4, so the text's Ki range 10.4-21.0 mixes an IC50 into a Ki range and omits the lower table Ki (7.34).

anchors.locator: II. Pharmacokinetics > A. Metabolism, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd being the running paragraph after the Fig. 1 legend)
anchors.extracted: Ketamine is extensively metabolised, first by nitrogen demethylation to norketamine, catalysed primarily by the liver cytochrome P450 enzymes CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 (stereoselective: CYP3A4 prefers the S form, CYP2B6 treats both about equally). Norketamine is then metabolised to the hydroxynorketamines and to dehydronorketamine; (2R,6R;2S,6S)-HNK formation is mainly by CYP2A6 and CYP2B6, and dehydronorketamine comes from norketamine mainly via CYP2B6 or non-enzymatically from 5-hydroxynorketamine.

anchors.locator: II > A. Metabolism, 5th running paragraph (the paragraph before Table 2)
anchors.extracted: After a 40-minute intravenous infusion of 0.5 mg/kg in patients with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder, peak plasma concentrations were 204.13 +/- 101.46 ng/mL (0.86 +/- 0.43 micromolar) ketamine at 40 minutes, 73.54 +/- 31.86 (0.33 +/- 0.14) norketamine at 80 minutes, 13.27 +/- 6.92 (0.06 +/- 0.03) dehydronorketamine at 110 minutes and 23.19 +/- 11.88 (0.097 +/- 0.05) for (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine at 230 minutes (Zarate et al., 2012a). In the parallel treatment-resistant bipolar depression group the peaks were 177.23 +/- 53.8, 69.96 +/- 19.98, 50.5 +/- 27.44 and 37.59 +/- 14.23 ng/mL at the same times. Norketamine, dehydronorketamine and (2R,6R;2S,6S)-HNK were the major circulating metabolites.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Pharmacokinetic comparison for (2R,6R) and (2S,6S)-HNK in humans and rodents), human rows
anchors.extracted: Humans, racemic ketamine 0.5 mg/kg as a 40-minute intravenous infusion, plasma: ketamine AUClast 873.5 h.ng/mL (3.67 h.micromolar) in major depression and 975.4 (4.10) in bipolar depression, against (2R,6R;2S,6S)-HNK AUClast 1038 (4.33) and 1366 (5.70), so total exposure to the metabolite pair exceeded exposure to ketamine in both groups. Cmax values as in the text. Header: values are mean +/- S.D. Source line: Zarate et al. (2012a) plus 'Unpublished data', so the AUC figures are partly unpublished.

The review states that there are important species differences in half-life, AUC, Cmax and clearance, and that the brain levels of ketamine and its metabolites after administration in people are not known, so direct comparisons are not straightforward.

anchors.locator: IV. Conclusions > A. (R)- and (S)-Ketamine as Antidepressants, last paragraph
anchors.extracted: The review states there are no published clinical studies assessing the antidepressant efficacy of R-ketamine in people with depression, and no published clinical studies directly comparing the antidepressant actions of the S and R forms with each other or either with the racemic mixture. S-ketamine was in phase III trials as an antidepressant at the time of writing.

Two authors are named coinventors on a patent for the use of (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine, (S)-dehydronorketamine and other stereoisomeric dehydro- and hydroxylated ketamine metabolites in depression and neuropathic pain; six authors, including the first and last, are named coinventors on a patent application for (2R,6R)- and (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine in depression, anxiety, anhedonia, suicidal ideation and post-traumatic stress disorder, with royalty shares assigned to the US government or the University of Maryland, Baltimore.

anchors.locator: IV. Conclusions > B. Utility of Ketamine's Hydroxynorketamine Metabolites as Drug Treatments, 1st paragraph, with III > A, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The proposal that the hydroxynorketamines carry part of the antidepressant action rests on rodent and in vitro work: metabolism is necessary for ketamine's full antidepressant action in mice and (2S,6S)- and (2R,6R)-HNK produce antidepressant-like behaviour without NMDA receptor inhibition at relevant concentrations (Zanos et al., 2016; Morris et al., 2017; Suzuki et al., 2017). The review's own listing of that evidence cites one independent supporting study (Pham et al., 2017a) and two independent studies against it (Shirayama and Hashimoto, 2018; Yang et al., 2017).

anchors.locator: I. Introduction > A. Clinical Therapeutic Effects, 1. Anesthetic (2nd paragraph) and 3. Antidepressant (last paragraph), with Table 1
anchors.extracted: Blood levels reached in people: peak plasma concentrations of about 1200-2400 ng/mL (5-10 micromolar) are needed for dissociative anaesthesia; the 0.5 mg/kg 40-minute infusion used for depression gives a maximum of about 185 ng/mL (about 0.78 micromolar), calculated by the review from Zarate et al. (2012a). Table 1 lists the same antidepressant row (0.5 mg/kg, 40-minute infusion; 185 ng/mL; 0.78 micromolar) but attributes it to Zarate et al. (2006), not 2012a. I recomputed both conversions with the review's molecular weight 237.73 and get 5.05-10.1 and 0.778.

anchors.locator: III > D. Cholinergic Receptors, 1st and 3rd paragraphs, with Table 3 (M1 mAChR and nicotinic rows)
anchors.extracted: Against the claim's 'above the blood levels reached in people': the review reports that Durieux (1995) found ketamine inhibited the M1 muscarinic receptor at clinically relevant concentrations (IC50 5.7 micromolar, rat receptor in Xenopus oocytes), and that ketamine blocked alpha4beta4 nicotinic receptors in Xenopus oocytes with IC50 0.24 +/- 0.03 micromolar (chicken receptor; Flood and Krasowski, 2000), complete inhibition at 10 micromolar. The review then states that because concentrations up to about 10 micromolar are within the clinically relevant range, some nicotinic subtypes may underlie ketamine's effects in vivo, and that other nicotinic subtypes are also sensitive at therapeutically relevant concentrations; Table 3 adds dehydronorketamine at the alpha7 nicotinic receptor at IC50 0.055 +/- 0.006 micromolar. Muscarinic Ki values in human cells are higher (M1 45, M2 294, M3 246 micromolar).

anchors.locator: III > B. Hyperpolarization-Activated Cyclic Nucleotide-Gated Channels, 2nd paragraph, with Table 3 (HCN1, DAT and L-type VDCC rows)
anchors.extracted: Also against 'about 10 to 1000 micromolar, above the blood levels reached in people': HCN1 inhibition is reported at EC50 8.2-15.6 micromolar for racemic ketamine and 4.1-7.4 micromolar for the S form (Chen et al., 2009), and the review treats this as possibly relevant to anaesthesia (ketamine anaesthesia was suppressed in HCN knockout mice). Table 3 further lists a dopamine transporter IC50 of 4.6 micromolar (rat striatum, Keita et al., 1996), an L-type calcium channel IC50 of 9.2 micromolar (bullfrog atrial myocytes) beside 1000 micromolar in pig trachea, and a sigma Ki of 0.15 micromolar (rat whole brain, Hustveit et al., 1995) beside the tens-of-micromolar sigma values the text discusses.

anchors.locator: III > E. Monoaminergic Receptors and Transporters, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, with Table 3 (D1-5R row)
anchors.extracted: The review sets against the dopamine account: two human imaging studies found no change in striatal D2 receptor binding (Kegeles et al., 2002, bolus 0.12 mg/kg then 70-minute infusion of 0.65 mg/kg per hour, mean plasma 0.59 +/- 0.22 micromolar; Aalto et al., 2002, 66-minute infusion, steady plasma 1.23 +/- 0.12 micromolar, healthy men); a D2 receptor antagonist did not block the psychotomimetic effects of a 0.23 mg/kg bolus or 0.65 mg/kg per hour infusion in people (Krystal and D'Souza, 2001); and Can et al. (2016) found no change in electrically evoked accumbal dopamine release in mice and no functional agonist or antagonist activity at any dopamine receptor subtype up to 10 micromolar. Table 3 shows that the receptor panel used human D1-D5 receptors expressed in HEKT or fibroblast cells, so the 'no activity up to 10 micromolar' result is a human-recombinant-receptor finding, not the mouse part of the study. Earlier studies had reported D2 affinity 0.055-1.0 micromolar and partial agonism (EC50 0.9 +/- 0.4).

anchors.locator: Article structure (headings I-IV) and Authorship Contributions
anchors.extracted: The article has no methods or search section: it runs Abstract, I. Introduction, II. Pharmacokinetics, III. Pharmacodynamics, IV. Conclusions, with no statement of a systematic search, inclusion criteria or appraisal of the studies tabulated. This matches the claim's framing that the figures are second-hand and not appraised, and that single reported values are presented as the primary studies gave them.

key_findings.correction: Metabolic pathway, stereoselectivity of CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, the hydroxynorketamine and dehydronorketamine routes, the minor hydroxyketamine and hydroxyphenyl routes and the P450-expression explanation for variability are all in II.A, paragraphs 1 to 3 and the two figure legends, as given.

All of it is in II.A, 4th running paragraph: major circulating metabolites, detection from 40 minutes after the end of the infusion, times to peak about 1.33 and 3.83 hours, S to R ratios 0.84, 1.0 and 0.67, Geisslinger 0.91 and the three five-day-infusion ratios 0.77, 0.71, 0.71. The 0.84 ratio is repeated in II.C as the locator says.

Every value matches (both patient groups, all four analytes, all four peak times, and the four AUC figures 873.5 and 975.4 against 1038 and 1366 h.ng/mL). Table 2's header does say mean plus or minus S.D. One addition worth making: Table 2's human row is sourced to 'Zarate et al. (2012a), Unpublished data', so the AUC figures that carry the metabolite-exceeds-parent comparison are partly unpublished.

All bioavailability figures and peak times match II.B, 1st paragraph. The paediatric figure is Hornik et al. (2013) as cited in the text, which is the citation error the card records as reporting issue 7.

Protein binding 10 to 50%, volume of distribution 3 to 5 l/kg, no interconversion of the enantiomers, and the statement that human brain levels are not known (II.D, last paragraph, which is the 7th running paragraph of that section).

Half-life 2 to 4 hours, 186 minutes and 19.1 ml/min per kg intravenously against 155 minutes and 23.2 intramuscularly, the 2 / 2 / 16 / about 80% excretion figures, the one-day against three-day detection, children about twice as fast, and S-ketamine 26.3 plus or minus 3.5 against 14.8 plus or minus 1.7 ml/kg per minute all sit in paragraphs 1 to 5 of II.D, as the locator says. Small point: the review attributes the 2 / 2 / 16% figures to five sources and only the 80% figure to Dinis-Oliveira (2017).

Content is right, locator is one paragraph short. In III.A the open-channel-blocker description is in the 1st paragraph, but the phencyclidine site within the pore, the trapping percentages (about 86%, >98%, 100%) and the Ki range 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar are in the 2nd paragraph; the S against R comparison is in the 3rd and the magnesium material with Yamakura et al. (1993) in the 4th. Locator should read: III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Table 3, NMDAR rows. Also: the review does not call the two human cortex values post-mortem (it says post-mortem only of the separate Oye et al. 1992 enantiomer samples), and the racemic rows include guinea pig and dog as well as rodent, cells and oocytes.

The occupancy figures (31% plus or minus 18% in people after the 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion; 32% plus or minus 6% in rats at 10 mg/kg intraperitoneally, both from Shaffer et al., 2014) are in the 3rd paragraph of III.A, the one after Table 3, not the 2nd. Values confirmed. The review does not state whether the spread is an SD or an SE. The gloss 'the review uses this to argue that the clinically used dose only partly occupies the receptor' is the card's reading: the review reports the maximum occupancy and the rat comparison and then turns to R-ketamine's potency as the challenge to the NMDA-receptor account.

Values confirmed, paragraphs off by one: the norketamine affinities are in the 6th paragraph of III.A and the dehydronorketamine and hydroxynorketamine material in the 7th (the 5th is the Dravid et al. 2007 subunit paragraph). One citation to correct: the finding that neither hydroxynorketamine inhibits NMDA-evoked currents up to 10 micromolar is Zanos et al. (2016), with Suzuki et al. (2017) for (2R,6R)-HNK; Morris et al. (2017) is binding, not currents.

The individual numbers are right (alpha4beta4 0.24, alpha3beta4 3.1, alpha7 about 17 to 20, HCN1 8.2 to 15.6 and 4.1 to 7.4, M1 45 against 5.7 with the expression-system explanation, opioid tens to hundreds, sigma 19 to 139, GABA-A hundreds, sodium and L-type calcium mostly hundreds to millimolar, no GABA-A binding in the human PET study), but two summary statements need correcting. First, 'other targets lie mostly outside clinically reached concentrations' is not what the review says of all of them: it reports that Durieux (1995) inhibited M1 at clinically relevant concentrations (IC50 5.7 micromolar), states that concentrations up to about 10 micromolar are within the clinically relevant range so some nicotinic subtypes may act in vivo, calls the alpha3beta4 values of 3.1 and 9.1 micromolar therapeutically relevant, and treats HCN1 inhibition (4.1 to 15.6 micromolar, against the 5 to 10 micromolar reached at anaesthesia) as possibly contributing to anaesthesia. Second, 'serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine transporters mostly above 60 micromolar' omits the lower tabulated values: dopamine transporter IC50 4.6 micromolar (rat striatum, Keita et al., 1996) and serotonin transporter IC50 18.8 and 20.2 micromolar (Martin et al., 1988, 1990). Sigma also has a tabulated racemic Ki of 0.15 micromolar outside the 19 to 139 range (see missed, below).

All five strands confirmed, and the card's separation of the Can et al. (2016) findings (no functional activity at any dopamine receptor subtype up to 10 micromolar, which Table 3 shows was measured on human receptors expressed in cells, and separately no change in evoked dopamine release in mice) is more accurate than the claim's wording. The content sits in the 2nd and 3rd running paragraphs of III.E; the 4th (dopamine transporter) is not part of this finding.

The 30-fold dose range, the absence of a brain-exposure difference, the absence of dissociation, ataxia and abuse liability in animal tests, and the two statements that no clinical study of R-ketamine in depressed patients and no clinical comparison of the enantiomers or of either against the racemate had been published are all at the stated places (IV.A, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; IV.B, 1st paragraph).

Doses, species, durations, the 24-hour reversal at low doses, the two primate findings, the tau findings in monkeys and mice and the two cross-sectional human imaging studies all match the three paragraphs of the Neurotoxicity subsection, and the review does call the relevance to people controversial and difficult to assess.

Timing (within 10 minutes of the start, subsiding within 40 minutes of the end), the contrast with 0.1 mg/kg, the pattern of preserved global cognition and immediate recall, the two studies in people with schizophrenia, the peripheral effects and the urological and memory findings with prolonged non-medical use are all as reported. The 0.1 mg/kg point is the one the card itself flags as internally inconsistent (reporting issue 4).

reporting_issues.note: Text does print 0.1 to 1442 ng/mL as 0.0004 to 0.031 micromolar for norketamine. I recomputed with the norketamine molecular weight 223.70: 1442 ng/mL is 6.45 micromolar and 0.1 ng/mL is 0.00045, so the lower bound is right and the upper is wrong by a factor of about 208, i.e. more than two orders of magnitude, as the card says. The ketamine pair converts correctly (2 ng/mL = 0.0084; 1204 ng/mL = 5.06).
The sentence on the five-day infusion names the same pair twice as the two major metabolites on day 3.

Text 2.36 plus or minus 0.18 micromolar against Table 2's 2.36 plus or minus 0.36, with the same 561.89 plus or minus 86.09 ng/mL in both (and 561.89/237.73 = 2.363, so the central value is consistent).

All three examples check out against Table 3: S-norketamine 0.87 and R-norketamine 0.60 (Morris et al., 2017) are tabulated but left out of the text's 1.70-2.25 against 13.0-26.46 contrast; the (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine range 10.4-21.0 takes 10.4 from an IC50 row and omits the tabulated Ki of 7.34; the dehydronorketamine ranges mix Ki with IC50 (S: Ki 38.95 with IC50 42.0, omitting Ki 29.7; R: Ki 74.55 with IC50 59.7, omitting Ki 42.1). Each omission does run in the direction of the contrast the text draws.
Psychoactive-effects subsection: little to no psychoactive effects at 0.1 mg/kg; abuse subsection: the same dose induced a mild euphoria.

The text calls the 100 to 250 ng/mL range for Krystal et al. (1994) estimated; Table 1's dissociation row prints it without that qualification beside measured values. The same pattern applies to the 0.1 mg/kg range (about 25 to 50 ng/mL) and to several other 'estimated from' concentrations in II.C.

The text says opioid-receptor inhibition by naloxone augmented ketamine's dissociative and cognitive effects in healthy volunteers, citing Krystal et al. (2006), whose reference-list title is about potentiation of low-dose ketamine effects by naltrexone. Mikkelsen et al. (1999), cited two paragraphs earlier, is the naloxone study.
Text cites Hornik et al. (2013); the reference list entry is Hornik CP et al. (2018).
379 plus or minus 71 and 389 plus or minus 74 are printed as ng/mg; dividing by the molecular weight 237.73 gives 1.594 and 1.636 micromolar, matching the printed 1.59 and 1.64, so ng/mL is meant.

All three sentences are present as described (deaths from ketamine alone very rare, no report of a lethal dose known to the authors, most if not all side effects dose dependent, transient and self-resolving), with no body of evidence reviewed for any of them.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' narrative-review checklist is the right instrument (METHODS 5.3: no validated instrument, stored as none-applicable), the overall judgment of high is not less severe than the worst domain, and I reach the same domain judgments. I read the article in full and found no search strategy, selection criteria or dates; the metabolite pharmacokinetics and pharmacology do rest largely on the authors' own laboratories, with Table 2 rows marked unpublished, on compounds they have patented (Footnotes); and the counter-evidence to the hydroxynorketamine account appears mainly as a parenthetical pointer (Shirayama and Hashimoto, 2018; Yang et al., 2017). I would add one point to the appraisal domain, not enough to change the judgment: the review repeatedly draws ranges from its own Table 3 in a way that mixes Ki with IC50 values and drops tabulated values (the card's reporting issue 3), which is an appraisal failure on its own evidence, not only on the primary studies'.

interpretation_gap.note: Agree with 'minor', and with both halves of the card's reading: the abstract and conclusions do label the metabolite evidence preclinical, while the safety sentences, the prolonged-elimination generalisation from what reads as a single person's three infusions, and the Future Directions feasibility statement go beyond what is reviewed. It is close to the boundary: placing 'most, if not all, side effects of ketamine are dose dependent, transient, and self-resolving' a few pages after the review's own account of ulcerative cystitis and lasting memory deficits with prolonged non-medical use is a substantive mismatch, and a reader who took that sentence alone would be misled. I would keep 'minor' only because it is confined to passing statements and the review's load-bearing conclusions are hedged.

missed: Table 1 attributes the antidepressant row (0.5 mg/kg, 40-minute infusion; 185 ng/mL; 0.78 micromolar) to Zarate et al. (2006), while the text states the value was calculated from Zarate et al. (2012a). The 2006 trial is not the source of that Cmax, so Table 1 points a reader to the wrong paper for the single most-cited concentration in the review.

Table 3's sigma rows are internally inconsistent: Hustveit et al. (1995) is listed with a racemic Ki of 0.15 micromolar, while the text reports 19 micromolar for the R form and 131 for the S form from the same study. A racemate cannot bind about 100 times more strongly than either enantiomer, and the 0.15 value sits far outside the 19 to 139 micromolar range the text (and key finding 9) give for sigma receptors.

The sentence carrying the racemic NMDA-receptor range 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar cites three sources with no matching racemic row in Table 3 (MacDonald et al., 1987, which has no row at all; Moaddel et al., 2013 and Bonifazi et al., 2015, which appear only under the enantiomers), and Table 3 also carries a racemic Ki > 10 micromolar (Georg and Friedl, 1991, in a rat glioma hybrid cell line) that falls outside the stated range without comment.

Tissue mismatch between text and table for norketamine: the text locates the S-norketamine Ki range in the spinal cord and the cerebral cortex, but Table 3's two matching rows are rat cortex and rat whole brain and there is no spinal-cord norketamine row.

Table 2's human AUC values, which carry the statement that exposure to the hydroxynorketamine pair exceeded exposure to ketamine, are sourced to 'Zarate et al. (2012a), Unpublished data'. The card's selection_effects notes unpublished rows in general, but this particular comparison is used in the claim and should be flagged as partly unpublished where it is reported (key finding 2).

Among the clinically relevant concentrations the review itself names, dehydronorketamine inhibits the alpha7 nicotinic receptor at IC50 0.055 micromolar (Moaddel et al., 2013, rat receptors in cells) - a metabolite potency two orders of magnitude below the concentrations reached in people, which the review offers as a possible non-NMDA route for metabolite effects. It belongs beside key finding 9's nicotinic figures.
